#4859. After Launching McGee & Co., Shea McGee Shares 8 Lessons for Opening a Store

My husband Syd and I are both lovers of retail, and have always known one day we’d have a McGee & Co. shop of our own. Over the years, we’ve spent a lot of time jotting down ideas for our own store. Our new flagship is a repository for all that knowledge that we’ve been squirreling away—but it also taught us a few lessons of its own.

Speaking to you now, on the other side of its debut, there are some things we only learned through actually doing. From the importance of developing a training manual to the do-or-die value of a soft launch, here are eight hard-won learnings from our McGee & Co. store launch.

It was important to us that the shop feel like the homes we create for our clients—layered and collected, with a variety of patterns and objects for your eye to explore. Despite the fact that the dollars-per-square-foot model is the traditional method of conceiving an in-store assortment, it was more important for us to remain true to ourselves with this first location: we’re a designer-led brand, not a merchant-led one.

“I’m getting to see our products through new eyes—and I was the one that concepted them!” says Shea. “When you see them in a store setting, pieces can have a lot more detail than you can see online.”

We started by coming up with the sections we envisioned, like a kids’ area, a kitchen zone, and so on. Then we created planograms to see how much we could actually fit, and reconciled with our merchandising team to see what made business sense. Sometimes, that meant pivoting from the early vision. A lighting gallery we had planned, for instance, ended up shifting: We loved the idea, but when we looked at the percentage of lighting to the rest of our sales, we could see clearly that it was a smarter business decision to use this space to showcase more furniture. Instead of the sprawling lighting gallery we had imagined, we created a moody lounge area that can flex to showcase different pieces.

We don’t think small: Our aspirations are to grow nationwide. But however much we scale, it’s critical that we not lose the warm, personal feeling that comes from a standalone store. As McGee & Co. grows its brick-and-mortar operation, that’s one of my biggest goals. And there’s another layer here, too: Being a personality-led business, the team members in our store aren’t just representing our brand—they’re representing me, for better or worse. The design world can sometimes feel closed-off and unapproachable, and it’s always been the McGee mantra—in our content, in our personality on social media, in how we work with clients—to be warm and accessible. Now that attitude needs to trickle down to our store associates, too.

Before we opened, I spent months developing a comprehensive training guide for our associates. It’s essentially Design 101, McGee-style, covering everything from how many inches I place a rug away from a wall, to how to pair and arrange accent tables, to how to layer bedding. We cover every level of the decorating process. Thank goodness for AI—it’s been a lifesaver: I’ll narrate as we go on our walk-throughs, and use those notes as the basis for the training manual. And it’s not a one-and-done deal. We’ll continue to add to this document as we evolve and grow.

Every issue, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching

Having that Design 101 established is a first step, but how do you ensure that the team is really internalizing the lessons? For us, the answer was checkpoints. As our design associates go through training and familiarize themselves with our ways of doing things, we hold check-ins with them to make sure that they’re absorbing our ways of operating. It’s the exact same as we do for the junior interior designers at Studio McGee: The checkpoints allow us to build up mutual confidence, with the aim for them to eventually fly on their own.

Shea plans to have the studio’s senior-level designers hosting regular check-ins with the shop’s design associates.

Personally dropping in myself can serve as another kind of checkpoint, too. With the flagship local, I’m able to stop by regularly in these early days to make sure that our standards are upheld, that our visuals are tight, and the operation is humming. That won’t work for us in every location, but it’s certainly a perk of opening up in our own hometown.

As much as I love a good plan, there’s nothing like real-time feedback to show you what’s working and what’s not. Which is why we kicked off our flagship back in September with a whisper and not a bang. We did a very soft launch with no announcement, no social post. We just opened the doors. As folks wandered in, we learned, and we tweaked. And two weeks later, we opened officially. That soft-launch period was vital for us in getting the kinks out.

One benefit of having had an ecommerce business for so long is that we have rich data on exactly where our customers are. That means that from day one, we already know where we need to open next. While launching in Salt Lake City was a logical place for our flagship, we’re already thinking ahead to how we’ll expand to some of our other biggest markets, like Texas and California.

Located in Salt Lake City’s Trolley Square, the “shop,” as Shea calls it, is 7,500 square feet.

We want to capitalize on the fact that the retail-ecommerce loop is an advantageous cycle: Where you have a retail store, your ecommerce sales lift. People who are aware of your product can go see it in person, give it a sit test, think about it, and then finish the sale online. In store, we can educate them, give them styling suggestions, and show off the quality of the product in ways we can’t online. Even for us, we’re discovering new things about our assortment by merchandising it in the store—we’re seeing it with fresh eyes, and we know our customers will too.

Aside from the obvious metric of profitability, to me, success in these early days means nailing down our systems and processes. It’s not the most glamorous side of this business, but it’s a must. I want to be able to say that we know what it takes to run a store and to make the shopper experience in it as smooth as possible. For instance, I want customers to know how to get to our free design services, and to have a great experience using them. If we can do that, we know we’re on our way to some of our loftier goals, too.

I’m not under any illusions here: This first store is a baptism by fire. Not only are we opening a flagship and planting seeds for our future locations—we’re also doing it in Q4, right before the holidays. But my hope is that at the end of it, we can catch our breath and take a moment to reflect on what worked, what didn’t, and then get to work fixing it. In this business, honesty with yourself is the only way up.

“The kitchen is a working kitchen,” says Shea, who envisions cooking demos and community events enlivening the space.

#4858. Here are the best electric bikes you can buy at every price level in November 2026

I’ve spent countless hours here at Electrek doing detailed hands-on testing of hundreds of electric bikes. Through thousands of miles of riding, I’ve been fortunate to learn these e-bikes inside and out, top to bottom and front to back. That long-term experience with real-world e-bike testing has helped me find the best electric bicycles on the market for just about any budget.

Below are some of the top e-bikes I’ve hand-tested for every price range, current as of November 2026. These are probably the best deals you’ll find all year on electric bikes, meaning this is the best time ever to get a new model! Check out the awesome e-bikes below, any one of which could become your next electric bike.

This list is divided into several price ranges. We’ll start with the best e-bikes under $1,000, then move on to the under-$2,000 category, under-$3,000 category, etc. The goal is to highlight some of my favorite models in various budget ranges to help you make the right decision based on your needs and budget.

The sub-$1,000 electric bike category is critical for a few reasons.

First, it’s pretty hard to produce a quality e-bike and sell it for under $1k. Most of the options in this price category make too many sacrifices in quality or longevity to earn a spot on this list as one of “the best.”

Second, many newly curious e-bike buyers just aren’t prepared to drop several thousand dollars on a brand-new concept, making this price range critical for many new e-bike shoppers.

Fortunately, we’ve found some excellent options for cheap electric bikes that can still save you some serious dough.

The Lectric XP LITE 3.0 was recently updated and is now quite likely the king of bang-for-your-buck electric bikes.

For a while now, the $999 Lectric XP 4 has reigned supreme in the budget electric bike category. That’s still a great bike, and we’ll discuss it next, but the more affordable $799 Lectric XP LITE3 is an even more wallet-friendly electric bike.

That new e-bike offers some great riding at under 800 bucks.

It’s a throttle-enabled Class 2 folding electric bike with 20″ wheels, a max speed of 20 mph (32 km/h), and a motor rated for 300W continuous and 819W peak. It’s not going to be the strongest hill climber in this list, but it does get going quickly on flat and modestly hilly terrain.

And the biggest features include quality hydraulic disc brakes, color LCD screen, turn signals, and even an optional Gates carbon belt drive system for an extra $100. Riders can also opt for a nearly double-sized battery for an extra $200.

This is the only e-bike in this price range that I know of with a 48V electrical system. All the other budget e-bikes under $800 use a 36V system and thus suffer from weaker power.

There are some things that you give up with this model, such as that the fenders aren’t included free. But for just $799, you’re still getting built-in lights, a hidden battery, large color LCD display and a lightweight folder. Plus it comes in lots of fun color options.

The Lectric XP4 is the undisputed best-selling electric bike in the US. The bike has racked up massive sales figures as riders flock to its extreme bang-for-your-buck. Simply put, it’s hard to find any other e-bike that offers this level of value!

The XP4 can get riders up to 28 mph (45 km/h) and now comes in either a 500W or 750W version, with respective battery sizes of 48V 10.4Ah and 48V 17.5Ah. The long-range version’s premium price tag ($1,299 vs the standard range model at $999) is perhaps even higher value than the already impressive base model.

Other upgrades include a new stronger rack design, torque sensor for smoother pedal assist, and improved hardware like the 8-speed transmission, hydraulic disc brakes, updated urban/trail hybrid-style tire tread, and a beautiful new TFT color screen.

The XP4 is hands-down the highest value e-bike I’ve ever tested and it’s quite obvious just how much time and effort went into building such a potent e-bike designed to fit so many different riders and tasks.

It’s hard to find a better combination of low cost and high performance anywhere in the e-bike market right now.

When Ride1Up launched the original Portola, it was pretty obvious what the game plan was: fire a shot across Lectric Ebike’s bow with a direct competitor to the Lectric XP line. By all accounts, Ride1Up nailed it with an impressive competitor. Now the company has come back with the next generation of the bike, this time attempting to take on both the XP line and XP Lite from Lectric. That’s thanks to two models, the Portola 02, and the stripped-down Portola 02 Lite.

The Ride1Up Portola 02 has a lot more going for it than just the attractive starting price of $895 for the Lite or $995 for the full-size bike with frame-integrated rack. The models offer great performance with a maximum speed of 28 mph (45 km/h) and good quality components including hydraulic disc brakes, torque sensor, front suspension, a built-in rear rack (except for the Lite), and a 750W motor.

There are two battery options available, either a 48V 10Ah or a 48V 15Ah, and the larger battery only costs an extra $100, so it’s quite worth the extra 50% range.

I love the sleek-looking frame and apparently, I’m not alone. Those who are on the hunt for a good-looking folding fat tire e-bike that doesn’t break the bank will likely find this to be one of the more fashionable options.

Once you bump up above the $1,000 limit, you start to see many more great options for e-bikes in a wide range of categories.

From electric cargo bikes to cruisers and even electric mopeds, there’s something for everyone in this price range.

The $1,249 JackRabbit OG2 is in one of these fuzzy areas between e-bikes and other e-rideables. In this case, it straddles the line between an electric bike and an electric scooter.

It more or less feels like an electric bike based on its ride geometry. However, the lack of pedals means that it could also be classified as an electric scooter, albeit a large-wheeled e-scooter.

But with those 20-inch wheels and bicycle seat, the JackRabbit OG2 rides much more like a small folding e-bike than an e-scooter. And its electronics match that of a light e-bike, too.

The 300W motor gets the little runabout up to 20 mph (32 km/h). The small 158 Wh battery only offers around 10 miles (approximately 16 km) of range, but is also conveniently small enough to easily keep a spare battery in a cargo pocket or even a small purse.

The biggest benefit of the JackRabbit is that it is so simple that the lack of frills keeps the weight down to just 25 lb (11.3 kg)! For an e-bike, that’s almost so light that it floats.

The company also released a higher power and larger battery capacity version too, which might be good for riders who want to push harder and go farther. For those that want to see a few more upgrades on this minimalist e-bike, the JackRabbit OG2 and XG might be more your size.

See my full review of the JackRabbit OG2 here.

We called the Lectric XPedition e-cargo bike a runaway success right from the start, and that’s exactly what it turned into. Now with the new Lectric XPedition 2.0 on the road, it’s better than ever.

With heavy-hauling weight capacity, the option for one or two batteries for extra long range, hydraulic disc brakes and torque sensor-based intuitive feeling pedal assist, this e-bike is dragging electric cargo bikes into the future.

The $1,399 Lectric XPedition 2.0 has turned the electric cargo bike market upside down, bringing a heavy-hitting cargo e-bike to market for an ultra-affordable price.

While it’s not the fanciest cargo e-bike on the market (you’ll find those in the $4,000-$6,000 price range further down this article), it’s definitely the best bang for your buck thanks to a combination of high value parts and reasonable pricing.

The Heybike Ranger 3 Pro is probably one of the best deals in full-suspension folding e-bikes right now. With a combination of a powerful motor, comfortable geometry, front & rear suspension, and a high-tech interface that includes NFC card unlocking, the Heybike Ranger 3 Pro is punching above its weight class.

In fact, that’s its main drawback, its weight. It’s a heavy bike, but the speed and power mean heavier motors and batteries, so you know you’re going to be carrying a more robust powertrain around with you.

But between the performance and the looks, this is one awesome comfortable ride that just doesn’t break the bank! I had a blast reviewing it, and I’ll bet you’ll have a blast riding it!

The $1,399 Aventon Soltera.2 is the latest version of Aventon’s beautiful city bike that offers some of the best quality fabrication that I’ve seen in this price range – or even in higher price ranges. It is offered in either a single-speed or seven-speed format.

The bike rolls on narrow tires for that efficient city ride, while still packing in a 500W motor.

The battery is a bit smaller at 36V and 10Ah, but the bike makes up for a smaller battery by being able to integrate it into the frame in a sleek and attractive package.

The beautiful color display also adds to the bike’s charm, as do the powerful headlight and frame-integrated tail light. There’s even an awesome companion app that lets your phone track your bike’s important stats. Basically, you’re getting a lot for $1,199 here!

Check out my in-depth Aventon Soltera.2 review here.

Ride1Up has proven itself as a high-value electric bike brand, focusing largely on efficient and speedy commuter e-bikes. While the company has many models in the $1,000 to $2,000 range, the $1,295 Ride1Up Roadster V3 is one of the best bang-for-your-buck options in the lightweight category.

This 500W-rated e-bike offers Class 3 performance, meaning you can hit speeds of up to 28 mph (45 km/h), or a still impressive 20 mph (32 km/h) if using the throttle. But sticking to pedal-assist means you get to enjoy that quality torque sensor for smoother pedaling. The bike even comes with an option for either a belt drive or a 10-speed Shimano transmission, and three frame sizes to choose from.

The V3’s design was updated with many new features, including a now-removable battery for even more convenient charging both on and off the bike. And with a sub-40 lb weight, it’s hard to beat this one on a pound-for-pound basis!

Check out my full review of the Ride1Up Roadster V3 here:

Lectric Ebikes expanded into larger territory with the launch of the Lectric XPeak2. It was the company’s first e-bike with a larger than 20″ wheel size, bringing some chunky 26×4.0″ tires into the company’s inventory.

The XPeak takes the form of a typical adventure-style fat tire electric bike. It features a hardtail design with a suspension fork, high-volume tires, hydraulic disc brakes, and a relatively large battery that is certified by the Swiss testing agency SGS to meet UL 2849 standards.

The bike is also tested to higher standards for ruggedness of the frame and fork than most e-bikes in this price range, meaning it’s likely going to last longer too. As far as fat tire adventure-style e-bikes go, there’s no better bang for your buck than the Lectric XPeak2.

The $2,295 Ride1Up Prodigy V2 Eco has brought new meaning to the phrase “low-cost mid-drive electric bike”, updating an already impressive e-bike with a new next-gen setup.

This e-bike sports a high-end German-manufactured Brose mid-drive motor and can hit speeds of up to 28 mph (45 km/h), yet is price similarly to much cheaper hub motor-based electric bikes.

It’s a perfect commuter e-bike for someone who wants high-quality parts like that German mid-drive motor with 90Nm of torque, hydraulic disc brakes, bright LED lights, included fenders, rear rack, and a very comfortable saddle. Plus, there’s a choice between a step-over or a mid-step frame to better fit a wider variety of riders.

This e-bike is easily worth another $700 more than the price tag, if not more. In fact, you’ll find many of these same components on e-bikes with $2,000-$3,000 price tags all over the place. So if you’re looking for a higher quality e-bike that doesn’t cost as much as a fancy bike shop e-bike, this is the one to consider.

The Ride1Up Vorsa is Ride1Up’s most versatile “SUV‑style” e‑bike yet, designed to transition seamlessly from commuting through city streets to loaded errands and light gravel or park paths. With a standard price around US $1,495, it delivers an exceptionally high‑value riding experience that often outperforms models far above its price range.

With a powerful 750 W rear‑hub motor producing a hefty 95 Nm of torque (and peaking over 1,400 W in real-world tests), the Vorsa accelerates comfortably and can maintain Class 3 speeds of up to 28 mph via pedal assist or 20 mph throttle thanks to its dual-sensor system and customizable display. Whether you’re hauling cargo or cruising commute lanes, the Vorsa delivers smooth, responsive power that feels natural and planted.

I love how well‑rounded the package is. Ride1Up outfits the Vorsa with a 100 mm suspension fork, comfortable ergonomic bars, multiple colors/frame styles (step‑thru or standard), and a modular rear rack rated for 440 lb total payload, which is expandable via Connect+ accessories. Hydraulic disc brakes, full fenders, integrated lighting, and passive features like UL‑certified batteries and Apple FindMy integration round out the build.

At just $1,695, the Ride1Up Vorsa is priced way below fair market value, which makes this an absolute steal of a deal.

Check out my Ride1Up Vorsa review here, and also check out the new expansion to the Vorsa line with lighter and heavier duty models built on the Vorsa platform.

The Marker is the first model unveiled by the e-bike brand spun out of Lectric eBikes, known as Monarc. The brand leverages Lectric’s size and buying power to bring higher end bikes than we typically see in the budget space – complete with higher shelf components – but at better prices and with better customer service.

The Monarc Marker is a powerful, Class 3-capable fat tire adventure e-bike with powerful four-piston brakes, a quality reverse arch suspension fork, Shimano CUES transmission, and comes with two batteries, all for an incredible reasonable MSRP of US $1,999.

Monarc also made waves by offering a 5-year warranty as well as 12-hour customer service five days a week, ensuring customers feel comfortable knowing they are buying from a company that will stick around to support riders long after the purchase is complete.

Learn more about the Monarc Marker here, or check out its current sale price here.

When Juiced returned with a vengeance after being saved by Lectric, the brand did so with two impressive new Scrambler models: a hard tail and a full-suspension bike. They’re both awesome moped-style e-bikes and handle great, but the full-suspension version definitely kicks things up a notch and allows for even wilder riding.

But since they share the same features and performance outside the rear suspension, either would make an awesome addition to your e-bike fleet. Basically, it’s a powerful yet street-legal e-bike that is designed for real-world riding, thanks in no small part to its designer, Austin Homes, being a seasoned competitive bike racer across multiple disciplines and bringing that keen eye to the Scrambler’s development.

By the time you surpass the $2,000 mark, you’re starting to get into serious e-bikes with serious performance or build quality.

If you’re spending this much, you’ll want to ensure you’re buying from a reputable company with top-notch products and service.

The Ride1Up TraiRush is the first actually quite good electric mountain bike that comes in at a budget price. It gives you a real German-made Brose motor, which offers good power matched with whisper-quiet performance. You get a dropper seat post and Maxxis Minion tires, Tektro Orion quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, and a 120mm Rockshox Judy Silver TK Air Fork.

The first time I took a ride on the Ride1Up TrailRush, I couldn’t believe just how good the bike felt, especially from a company known for its wide array of commuter and street-oriented electric bikes. But Ride1Up was founded by cyclists at heart, and so they know what it means to build a good bike, regardless of category. At $2,095, this is a steal for just great parts.

I love the $3,299 Priority Current electric bike so much that it has become one of my daily riders. It’s the one I grab when I’m doing city riding and I know I want to be pedaling.

While the original version was already a great bike, the new Current Plus adds some key improvements, such as an included throttle and a nearly 50% larger capacity battery for more range. The throttle is great in a pinch, but the bike is also just so much fun to pedal thanks to a torque sensor-based pedal assist that provides natural-feeling assistance up to a fast 28 mph top speed.

The internally geared rear hub combined with a Gates belt drive system and powerful hydraulic disc brakes make this a very nice e-bike for the price. Plus that mid-drive motor offers tons of torque (140 Nm!) for climbing hills or accelerating quickly.

I’m also a fan of the built-in lights and included fenders, not to mention the punchy hydraulic disc brakes and Goodyear tires.

Mid-drive electric bikes aren’t cheap, but the price is definitely a fair one for this e-bike.

I’m not normally a carbon fiber, drop bar, race bike kind of guy. But then again, that’s usually because those types of bikes are way out of my price range… until now.

The Ride1Up CF Racer1 brings carbon fiber road e-bikes to the common man, offering both a traditional road bike and a gravel bike edition.

At under 29 lb (13 kg), these e-bikes are some of the lightest around. I picked one up with my index finger and was shocked at how easily it left the ground.

To get there, that meant a relatively low-power motor and a smaller battery were required. But for the folks that ride these types of bikes, a big motor and heavy battery probably aren’t on their wishlist anyway. Instead, a simple extra boost, as if you’ve always got a tailwind, helps augment your own pedaling.

For just $2,295, there’s no better deal out there for a budget-friendly carbon fiber road e-bike.

This full-suspension electric moped-style e-bike is a masterclass in high performance electric bike design. Sure, it’s an obvious SUPER73 imitation, but it’s a really well done imitation.

It handles well, it’s got great rubber between you and the road, the suspension gives a comfortable ride, and it’s got plenty of extra power.

Despite the 750W label, the e-bike can be unlocked to make use of nearly 1,500W of peak power. I was able to reach a top speed of 37 mph (59.5 km/h) during my testing (not on public streets!).

But the bike ships in Class 2 mode with a 750W limit and 20 mph (32 km/h) maximum speed, meaning you’ll have to contact the company to request an unlock for the bike to be used above Class 2 speeds and power levels.

All in all, the $2,395 Ride1Up REVV1 FS is an amazing e-bike for anyone who wants a moped-style ride with full-suspension, high quality 4-piston hydraulic disc brakes and a design that rides almost like a motorcycle, yet in a bike form factor.

Check out my complete Ride1Up REVV1 FS review here.

The Tern Quick Haul is an electric cargo bike from the famed cargo e-bike company Tern. It holds the distinction of being the most affordable model in Tern’s lineup.

That says a lot, because Tern is known for its high-quality e-bikes that are built to be ridden every day for real-world errands, carpool duty, and more. These e-bikes are meant to replace cars, and they do just that for many riders. With a huge list of accessories, you can outfit a Quick Haul for just about any job.

The Tern Quick Haul features a mid-drive Bosch motor, hydraulic disc brakes, Tern’s vertical parking rack, and a relatively lightweight but high utility design that is meant to carry just about anything in your life.

We had the chance to test a pair of Quick Hauls at Eurobike in Frankfurt last year, which you can learn more about here.

Motor: Bosch Active Line Plus mid-drive motorTop speed: 20 mph (32 km/h) with pedal assist (no throttle)Range: Up to 60 miles (96 km), less when riding in highest powerBattery: 400Wh, removable/lockableWeight: 50 lb (22.8 kg)Price: $2,999

When it comes to fast, powerful electric mopeds on a budget, it’s hard to compete with the $2,399 Ariel Rider X-Class. This is the e-bike I usually recommend when someone simply wants the most power and speed for the least amount of money.

The impressive performance comes from a powerful 1,000W motor that actually puts out closer to 2,000W of peak power. It can be limited to 20 mph if you’d like, but I got it up to 36 mph in unlimited mode.

The bike rolls on 20″ moto-style wheels and comes with nice parts including hydraulic disc brakes, a bench seat, dual suspension, and a big moto-style headlight.

You can see my full review of the Ariel Rider 52V X-Class here.

The Xtracycle Hopper is something of a Goldilocks cargo bike, in my opinion. It’s not as big as a traditional long tail cargo bike, but it’s still big enough to carry multiple kids or a week’s worth of groceries.

It’s also not as pricey as the expensive $5-7k bike shop cargo e-bikes, yet it’s much higher quality than the typical direct-to-consumer cargo e-bikes.

I’ve tested it for all sorts of cargo jobs and even put my friends and family on it to take their kids to school and let me know how it works for them. Everyone has come away impressed with the ride feel, which seems much more like a traditional bike than a bulky cargo bike.

For the money, the Xtracycle Hopper offers incredible value and much higher quality construction than you’d get with entry-level brands.

Check out my full Xtracycle Hopper review here.

Above $3.5k, you’re entering some seriously dedicated e-bike territory.

These e-bikes either feature top-shelf components like drivetrain and brake parts, or pack in so much power that they couldn’t possibly be priced any lower.

Either way, you’re not in Kansas anymore. You’re heading down the e-bike rabbit hole.

Tern is renowned for building high-quality electric bikes that double down on utility features. The newly updated Tern HSD is the company’s more affordable utility e-bike, offering many features you’ll find on its higher-end GSD but at a price that more riders can stomach.

The HSD uses small 20″ wheels and includes a folding stem, making it nice and compact. But taking it one step further, Tern outfitted it with its innovative rack that lets you park the bike on its tail, meaning it takes up barely more space than a coat rack in the corner of a room.

The bike’s Bosch mid-drive and high capacity batteries provide a high-end e-bike drive, and they are matched with a variety of performance drivetrain options that you can select from, depending on how high you want to spec the bike.

Whether you’re ferrying around kids or buying a week’s worth of groceries, the HSD is a solid option.

Check out my detailed first ride experience on the Tern HSD here.

The Xtracycle Swoop ASM is one of those electric cargo bikes that makes you rethink the entire category.

Not only does it include high-quality components and fancy features like automatic shifting paired with a high-end Shimano mid-drive motor, but it also just feels like you’re riding a normal-sized bike instead of a long and awkward cargo e-bike.

I found I can even ride it without my hands on the bars because it tracks so straight and rides so stable. That’s a feat you can’t pull off with most budget cargo e-bikes since they aren’t designed with proper bicycle geometry. But Xtracycle is a true cyclist’s cargo e-bike company, and so they understand proper bicycle design.

Check out my full review of this incredibly high-end and comfortable-to-ride cargo e-bike here.

When it comes to all-wheel-drive electric bikes, the $3,299 Ariel Rider Grizzly is one of my favorites.

This incredible e-bike is really more of a small electric motorcycle. It uses two high-power motors – one in each wheel – to offer speeds in the mid-30s and acceleration that will get you there in the blink of an eye.

Full suspension and hydraulic disc brakes make this an e-bike that handles well at any speed, and the bright red paint job looks as aggressive as the e-bike feels. It even comes with footpegs pre-installed so you can carry a passenger with you.

Plus it’s got double batteries to feed those two power-hungry motors, so you’ll be able to ride this e-bike pretty darn far too, as long as you aren’t too demanding from the throttle.

Check out my full in-depth review of the epic Ariel Rider Grizzly e-bike here.

The Priority Skyline builds upon Priority Bicycles’ legacy of creating high-performance, low-maintenance e-bikes and ups the ante with more premium parts than we’ve ever seen on a Priority e-bike before.

The show stopper here is the inclusion of Pinion’s 12-speed automatic gearbox, which smartly shifts gears without the rider ever having to think about it. You can personalize your shift points to dial in the ride, and let the centrally-mounted gearbox do the rest. The carbon belt drive transfers your pedal power while a 750W rear hub motor brings the extra power riders need.

There are also high-quality hydraulic brakes, a great suspension fork, and a big battery for long range in the city. Rear rack and complete fenders come standard, as do the built-in LED lights and adjustable handle-bar stem.

See my full review of the Priority Bicycles Skyline here.

You just couldn’t stop, could you? I showed you plenty of awesome e-bikes that didn’t cost most of a paycheck. But you just haaaaaaad to keep going.

Fine, here they are. These are some of the most expensive e-bikes out there that we’ve tested and that I’d actually recommend someone buying, if you can pony up the cash.

When it comes to ultra-premium folding electric bikes, there’s only one name that comes to my mind: GoCycle. These are the most impressive folding e-bikes I’ve ever seen. And they better be – they were designed by a former McLaren engineer.

Between the carbon fiber work, single-sided wheels, high-tech tires, trippy LED dot display, innovative rear suspension, and completely enclosed drivetrain, there’s a lot of high-end stuff going on here.

The speed will vary from 15-20 mph depending on which country you buy the bike in, but the performance is only part of the equation. The quick folding and light, compact design of the e-bike is the real winner here.

Check out my full review of the GoCycle G4i+ here.

The FREY EX Pro is a high-end electric mountain bike with crazy high power. It uses the same motor as the CSC FT1000MD we featured above (the Bafang M620 mid-drive), but cranks up the current to provide closer to 1,500W of power.

It’s enough to destroy chains if you aren’t careful. We know. Several of us here at Electrek have done it.

The FREY EX Pro not only features high-end parts like a RockShox Lyric fork and Magura MT5e hydraulic brakes, but it even comes with dual batteries so you can ride farther and stay on the trails longer.

I’ve personally taken this e-bike back UP a downhill mountain bike course – that’s how powerful it is.

It may be expensive, but it saves you several thousand dollars compared to many European electric mountain bikes with similar components but a fraction of the power in the FREY.

See my full review of the FREY EX Pro here.

The Tern GSD improves upon the Tern HSD with even more capability and even nicer components. There are multiple versions that can take you up to nearly $10k, but even the lower-tier versions are not “low tier,” if you know what I mean.

Parts like automatically engaging electric locks, 10-speed Shimano Deore transmissions, Magura MT5e quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, and more set these e-bikes apart from the rest of the pack.

If you’re getting a Tern GSD, you’re getting a fully qualified car replacement. There are many people who use these instead of buying a second car. When you look at it like that, the price suddenly seems pretty reasonable.

Check out our full review of the Tern GSD here.

#4855. How to Open a Retail Store, Win Customers, and Build a Business That Lasts

Even in the age of one-click shopping, opening an actual brick-and-mortar retail store is a dream for many designers. There’s something almost romantic about creating an entire environment where customers can sit on the sofas, feel the fabrics, or pick up a last-minute gift on their way to a party. It’s an opportunity to bring your brand to life and connect with customers in a way a website never can.

But opening a store requires a big leap of faith. Even if you have a loyal customer base, there’s something different about building a store. You have to think about everything from foot traffic to merchandising to hiring staff, and much more.

These are questions I’ve been wrestling with myself. Almost two months ago, after years of nurturing a thriving e-commerce business, my husband Syd and I unveiled our McGee & Co. flagship in our homebase of Salt Lake City. This project has been a goal of ours for a long time. We’ve been collecting ideas for years to ensure that whenever it opened, our physical retail operation would hold up to the high standards of service and design that we expect from every other part of our business. This project has had me thinking about retail at every hour of the day, mulling over some big questions... How do we translate a digital brand into a physical space for selling? How do we nurture customers and ensure they return? And how do we map our knowledge so that we can repeat our successes as we scale?

This guide, produced with our friends at AD PRO, distills some of the wisdom from our own experiences, as well as from a few insiders elsewhere in the industry. I’ll share some of the thinking and practical decisions behind our shop, from our merchandising strategy to how we recruited and trained our employees.

Next, AD PRO contributor Lila Allen speaks to me and my team, as well as professionals from retailers like Lawson-Fenning, Il Buco Vita, Tailor-Made Textiles, and ABC Carpet & Home, about how they cultivate customer loyalty over the long term. When access to product and knowledge is seemingly unlimited across the internet, we all agree: Earning trust and becoming a destination for discovery takes a lot of care. But it pays off. Relationships might be the most precious resource we have.

Then, contributor Margaret Borden catches up with the creatives behind some of this year’s buzziest shops—from a jewel-box fashion boutique in Paris to a bright, inviting kitchen and home goods shop in New York City—to glean their merchandising tips and tricks.

Whether you’re a designer thinking about hanging your own retail shingle, or you’re simply looking for a fresh perspective on the landscape of selling in 2026 and beyond, I hope this report will give you plenty of inspiration for the year ahead.

#4853. Falling Short In Life

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

We all fall short in life, and maybe that’s a good thing. Keeps us close to the Terra Firma.

Forgiveness of self and others, and the drive to press on in tough, wrenching times are coins of life. Pulitzer Prize-winning poet and journalist the late Carl Sandburg said years ago, “Time is the coin of life. It’s the only coin you have, and only you can determine how it will be spent.”

And that’s not pocket change. It’s a road map to success, though one that takes great persistence. I know firsthand from my life challenges. At 76 now, I’ve learned it’s not so much about the fall, but when and how you get back up—a humbling directive, though one that has helped me persevere through critical memory loss and advancing cancer, as others would know in their own trials.

I learned more about this recently in symbolic ways from my beautiful 40-year-old daughter Colleen, a writer and a teacher. November 16 was the 38th birthday of my late son Conor, who died several years ago from grand mal seizures and other issues. Conor traveled with me cross-country as a “guard dog,” as he called it, for speeches related to my book, On Pluto: Inside the Mind of Alzheimer’s. We were close, and in heavenly ways, closer now.

In a Facebook post on Conor’s birthday, shared also with son Brendan, Colleen—struggling through the emotion of this loss—wrote words that deeply touched my wife Mary Catherine and my soul—words that may touch you in losses in your lives.

Colleen wrote: “Happy Heavenly Birthday to my little brother, Conor, and my guardian angel. Your birthday is always especially hard for me because it makes me think of all the ‘could-haves’ and ‘should-be’s.’ But I feel you in the little things, the unexpected signs, and the moments that seem too coincidental to be anything else. I talk to you, I look for you, and I like to think you’re never far away.“Losing someone changes the way you look at life and the people around you. It reminds you that everyone is carrying something we may never see. That life is incredibly fragile, that tomorrow is never promised, and that we don’t always get another opportunity to say what we wish we had said. “I’ve learned how important it is to give people grace. To forgive, to let go of what weighs us down, to be kinder than we think we need to be, and to remember that none of us get through life without making mistakes. We don’t have to agree with everyone’s choices to show them compassion. We don’t have to understand someone’s struggles to remind them they’re not alone.“Make the phone call. Send the text. Forgive when your heart is ready. Ask a second time if someone says they’re okay, but something tells you otherwise. Tell people you love them while you have the chance.“I hope you’re proud of me, Conor. I hope you see how hard I’m trying. And I hope you know that no matter how much time passes, you will always be a part of me. Keep sending those signs. I’ll keep looking for them.“Love you, always, Conor. Until we meet again, Colleen.”

As I reflect on Colleen’s comments and Conor’s birthday, I am reminded again that it is crucial to rise from the falls of life. And I’m trying.

Over several months, the Women’s Health team, led by lifestyle director Lindsay Geller, researched the bestselling, most popular vibrators for women based on thousands of product reviews and sex therapist recommendations. “With any vibrator you’re using, you’re going to want to make sure you’re cleaning it after every session,” Richmond explains. A dirty vibrator can hold bacteria and germs—which, needless to say, can seriously kill the mood.

Generally speaking, expensive products are usually made from better, more body-safe materials. Ultimately, “a good-quality vibrator from a good-quality company is a good investment,” says Mintz. That said, it’s okay to try a few mid-priced toys of different categories before splurging on your new go-to luxury product, she adds.

On the flip side, water can also dull the intensity of a toy’s vibrations. “One of the reasons many people don’t like to have sex or use a vibrator in water is because it’s harder to feel things—but for somebody who is very sensitive, it could actually work to their benefit,” Laino adds. #4850. In Jordyn Woods-Towns’s NYC Home, Every Day is Knicksmas: “The Whole House Is Knicks-ed Out Already!”

The most wonderful time of the year holds a special place in Jordyn Woods-Towns’s heart—and no, we’re not talking about the start of basketball season. The fashion designer got engaged to Knicks phenom Karl-Anthony Towns on Christmas Eve 2025, and after a whirlwind 2026 including an NBA championship win for the New York NBA team (possibly courtesy of her viral accessory-turned-amulet) and a clifftop wedding replete with stunning details, the couple can’t wait to create festive memories as husband and wife.

“This is my first married Christmas,” Woods-Town tells AD. “I’ve only been married three months, but it’s our first holiday season, so I definitely need to try to figure out what our new traditions are.”

The newlywed reveals that she created an entire PowerPoint presentation to prep attendees for her bachelorette party, so you’d best believe she appreciates a little organization when it comes to getting in the spirit for big days. Planner that she is, Woods-Towns linked up with design marketplace Minted for her first family Christmas card and a curated suite of picks to welcome one particularly merry and bright yuletide season of life. Below, AD gets her take on holiday colors, basketball-themed decor, and more.

In anticipation of the holiday season, Woods-Towns teamed up with Minted to curate a selection of festive stationery and decor.

Architectural Digest: Have you always been a big holiday person?

Jordyn Woods-Towns: Every single season, I decorate. On Valentine’s Day I have the girls over to do a charcuterie board with salami roses and chocolate covered strawberries. Karl and I went crazy for Halloween; we turned the entire front yard into a whole different space with a graveyard and a 20-foot-tall skeleton. On Christmas, I love a theme.

For a couple years I went with a Candy Cane Lane vibe and now I’m in my chic New York era. I love a Ralph Lauren Christmas. I love the natural linen and natural materials. I’ve been really into natural florals, textural things. I love feathers, incorporating some ostrich feathers throughout—I do a lot of that with my brand, and I feel like feathers are really having a moment right now.

In New York it’s been hard because I don’t drive and I don’t have my car. I can’t just run down to HomeGoods, grab something, and come back!

What’s your decor looking like this year?

I’ve been really into all one shade. There were a lot of greens in our wedding and green is my color of the season.

Woods-Towns is leaning toward florals and green for holiday decorating this year.

The tree’s already green. It could be kind of cool, full green-on-green. Now I’m the Grinch. [laughs]

With your Christmas Eve engagement last year, the holiday is a sweet part of your love story. What sorts of traditions are you looking forward to starting with Karl?

I started with the holiday card with Minted. This is our first holiday card as a family. Obviously after you have kids, it kind of changes, but right now we’re at a time where life is just… he has a [Christmas Day] game and so we’re like, “Okay, we’re living the young, fast life.” But as time goes on, as our marriage goes on, we’re going to build different traditions. We love to be with our family and I always cook every holiday, so I’ll definitely be cooking after the game.

Is there a signature dish you like to serve?

Karl’s a picky eater. He loves chicken, so some version of chicken. He’s never had beef or pork or anything in his whole entire life. It’s just us, so some type of chicken and sides. Pretty simple.

I wanted to use a photo from our wedding that really felt like us, something that not everyone has seen, to tie in our whole year. It was a green marbled border design with gold foil border by Jenna Holcomb. There are those shades of green, since there’s a lot of green incorporated into our wedding. Olive is very timeless, and it felt chic and like us, like something that people could keep. I don’t want to say everyone’s going to want to put a photo of us in their house, but I know our family [will].

The Towns family’s holiday card. The design is “Marbled” by Jenna Holcomb.

Are you hosting bigger parties this season or just keeping it more intimate with the celebrations?

No huge parties, just because I don’t have the capacity to do that right now, but definitely getting the family together. We don’t have a huge family, so it should be pretty intimate, hopefully doing something with the team getting together. I think one of the girls was talking about doing a holiday party—even though I love to be the host, I don’t mind just showing up.

I would say it’s all in the details. I think through everything. But overall, it’s about the vibe that you’re bringing, the energy, and what you’re putting out. People remember the music, the food, and how they felt.

It’s been a busy 2026 for Woods-Towns between then-fiancé Karl-Anthony Towns’s successful championship run with the New York Knicks and her August wedding, but she’s keeping her energy high heading into holiday party season. “I feel like there’s an event every other day. But it’s not going to be like this forever. I had to change my mindset from, ‘Wow, I’m so tired,’ to, ‘Wow, I’m so lucky to be able to do this.’”

Are you planning on sprinkling any Knicks Easter eggs throughout your home decor or in your gifting this year?

There’s so many Knicks things in my house that it’s hard to escape. It’s already everywhere, the whole house is Knicks-ed out already! But I don’t mind Knicks-themed gifting—people love the Knicks.

Karl’s very hard to gift for, and his birthday’s actually right before the holidays. So it’s hard to figure out two really good gifts in a short amount of time. Gift giving is one of my love languages, and I love getting people things that they really can utilize in their everyday life. I need to think about that.

How else do you get in the holiday spirit at home?

I already bought Christmas pajamas and I already watched The Grinch twice with my niece and nephew two days ago. So I’m ready!

#4848. How the Film 'Anatomy of a Fall' Can Help You Build Empathy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

One of my favorite psychologists and the founder of humanistic psychology, Carl Rogers, saw empathy as one of “the most delicate and potent tools” we have as humans, and definitely not a weakness. The ability to take another person’s perspective and understand their thoughts, feelings, and experiences captures the fundamental meaning of empathy. We can also categorize empathy into two types: cognitive and emotional. In the simplest terms, emotional empathy means feeling what someone else feels; cognitive empathy means understanding what they feel.

The best part of empathy is its accessibility. We are naturally inclined toward empathy, but sometimes we turn it off or shut it out because it we may feel too much and become overwhelmed. It doesn’t have to immobilize us. If that were the case, therapists would never leave the house. We can learn to empathize with and feel for others while still setting boundaries that allow us to get on with our day-to-day lives.

Empathy can serve three key functions in our lives:

(1) Empathy expands our imaginative capacity.

(2) Empathy creates an ethical understanding with another person, creating trust.

(3) Empathy promotes change, especially in therapy, through creating insight.

Creative empathy is essential to our daily life because it enhances our ability to generate new ideas, knowledge, and ways of being in the world. Empathy-building activities in the classroom help students improve their creativity and critical thinking. Empathy can make meaningless activities significant and fun. Empathy helps us see problems from different angles, which can help creative performance.

For instance, a screenwriter must imagine not just what a protagonist wants, but how every character experiences the same moment differently. By empathizing with the different characters’ fears, hopes, and insecurities, a movie avoids clichés, creates richer, more complex characters, and connects better with audiences.

On the other hand, cognitive empathy enhances our ability to understand and express emotions and ideas. Research has found a relationship between cognitive empathy and almost all areas of creativity except science and engineering, where logic and reason dominate. The relationship between creative achievement and empathy shows that cognitive empathy has significant positive effects in visual arts, creative writing, inventions, scientific discovery, and the culinary arts.

Anatomy of a Fall (2023) is a French film directed by Justine Triet that is an excellent watch for tapping into your creative empathy. If you don’t know the Oscar-winning film, it is an almost Hitchcockian-like thriller that blurs the line between truth and fiction. Sandra Voyter (Sandra Hüller) is a writer who is put on trial for the death of her husband, whom she claims committed suicide.

As you watch, try these three exercises to tap into your creative empathy:

1. Shift your perspective: Think about how someone else might interpret this situation and Sandra’s character differently.

2. Change your perspective: As you watch Anatomy of a Fall, examine everyone’s thoughts, beliefs, and motivations rather than their emotions. Ask, “What is Sandra trying to protect? What does she believe about truth?”

3. Dive into unfamiliar perspectives: Instead of asking if Sandra is guilty, ask, “What does each character believe happened? Why would that version feel necessary to them?”

Creative empathy isn't just a luxury for screenwriters, but it's something we all need and crave. We need it to stay flexible, resilient, connected to others, and feel alive. In everyday life, as a parent, you empathize with your teenager’s need for independence rather than control; you may impose fewer rules and reach creative agreements—not punishment or lecturing. In that way, you let them develop the autonomy they need to succeed in life and set compassionate boundaries to help them achieve it.

Cuff, B. M. P., Brown, S. J., Taylor, L., & Howat, D. J. (2016). Empathy: A Review of the Concept. Emotion Review, 8(2), 144-153. https://doi.org/10.1177/1754073914558466

Levitt, H. M., et al. (2022). Learning Clinical and Cultural Empathy: A Call for a Multidimensional Approach to Empathy-Focused Psychotherapy Training. Journal of Contemporary Psychotherapy: On the Cutting Edge of Modern Developments in Psychotherapy, 52(4), 267–279.

Rogers, C. R. (1975). Empathic: An unappreciated way of being. The Counseling Psychologist, 5(2), 2-10.

#4847. Going the distance: these electric semi trucks cover over 600 miles EVERY DAY

“Sure, diesel is high, but electric trucks don’t work.” It’s a common refrain these days – especially from people selling diesel trucks. Perception lags reality, however, and the reality is that these electric semi trucks are covering more than 600 miles per day, seven days a week.

Over the course of the last year, Hendrik Müller, managing partner of DEFRU Logistik GmbH has transformed his company’s shipping fleet, switching thirty of their HD prime movers (semi trucks) to electric power and immediately putting the Mercedes-Benz eActros 600s to work, covering 1,000 km (~620 miles) of German highways each and every day.

Benjamin Budick, a Senior Manager, Own Retail Mercedes-Benz Trucks Dortmund & Haan, took to LinkedIn to announce the successful deployment, and posted some great pictures of the handover showing the big Mercedes trucks in full DEFRU livery.

Mercedes’ eActros 600 packs a whopping, 621 kWh battery that helps the trucks cover 500 km per charge, allowing fleets to move goods between ports and regional fulfillment centers, charging along the way, or while they’re getting loaded and unloaded at their destination, all the while saving the fleet serious money – even before the latest Iran War sent diesel prices skyrocketing.

That big battery sends electrons to Mercedes-Benz’s proprietary electric drive axles, which deliver 1.61 kWh / mile efficiency while rolling out at an average of 36 metric tons (~79,400 lbs.) combined vehicle weight – specs that rivals the theoretical efficiency claims of the Tesla Semi. Except in the real world. And in winter.

The eActros is a serious beast. As mentioned there are many configurations and they seem to work well in Europe. I've seen one that was configured with 620kWh battery, on one side a MCS port plus a CCS2 port (so thats either 1.2MW or 600kW charging options) and on the other side a CCS2 port.

In Europe with CCS, 350kW chargers are easy to find, 400kW are becoming more common and 600kW models are starting to arrive, therefore with the limitations on driving hours and speeds, the eActros really is an all day every day truck.

Of course if you are in the far North of Europe and are allowed to haul 60 tonnes, Scania have made a complete monster of a truck with over 800kWh of battery!

The company recently expanded its eActros lineup to include over 40 possible configurations, giving customers a choice of two cab designs, two or three battery packs, multiple wheelbases and new axle configurations, covering everything from short-haul drayage to serious, off highway vocational work.

#4844. 9 Best Small Sectional Sofas That Are Truly Stylish (2026)

A sprawling living room might be the dream, but having a small space doesn’t preclude you from being able to stretch out on the couch. Sectionals specifically designed for smaller rooms prove that cozy movie nights and afternoon naps aren’t reserved exclusively for those with a massive floor plan. In fact, choosing a sectional with the right proportions stands to make a smaller room feel larger. There’s no reason to settle for a hodgepodge of chairs and ottomans when a thoughtfully selected sectional can transform every seat into the best seat in the house.

Being mindful of a space’s dimensions is always important when shopping for furniture, but especially so with a small room, where every inch may matter. Still, a variety of clever configurations—including L-shaped sectionals designed to nestle into corners, modular designs that are easily rearranged, and sofas with reversible chaises that give you more flexibility—cater to seemingly every layout. Add in performance fabrics, washable slipcovers, and supportive cushions, and you’ve got a recipe for some seriously comfortable yet compact lounging. Ahead, we’re sharing our favorite sectionals for small spaces that ensure every square foot counts.

The best-selling Abisko sectional from Article is made even more beautiful by colorful, performance velvet upholstery. Suitable for those with little ones and pets running around, the fabric is non-absorptive, meaning spills and crumbs won’t stay embedded in its weave. Two orientations—chaise and L-shaped—allow you to Tetris its silhouette into your space as you see fit.

Instead of opting for a giant L-shaped sectional that will take up the entire room, aim for something with a smaller footprint. Available in performance fabric and three leg finishes, this sectional couch is ideal for a tiny living space and a major upgrade from a smaller loveseat thanks to the chaise addition. While not an official fold-out sleeper sofa, the back cushions flop back to give you enough space should you be inclined to nap. Contributor David Kaufman, who tested it out for us, calls it “a great starter sofa for a first home or apartment that you won’t have to send to a landfill when you’re ready to move.”

Similar to the Thuma sectional contributor Evan Russum told us “feels solid and durable,” the Essential Sofa follows the brand’s signature simple-but-considered aesthetic with a minimalist silhouette,rounded cushions, and a grounded wooden base. Raised armrests add sculptural presence without overwhelming a small living room, while the detachable ottoman lets you switch between a left- or right-facing chaise—so everyone can have a turn on their favorite side of the sofa.

Not your average grey couch, AllModern’s Jossa sectional is minimalist in looks but generous on comfort, thanks to its dense foam padding that offers plenty of support without feeling stiff. Easy to de-assemble, the modular design allows the sofa to evolve with your seating needs. Craving two separate lounge chairs? Done. Prefer a love seat? Just slide the two larger seats side-by-side. Today’s layout doesn’t have to be tomorrow’s.

The slim arms and low profile on this this reversible three-piece sectional make the Unwind especially suitable for a limited living area as it doesn’t monopolize the space. Five neutral color variations all come in a linen blend, but olive’s grounding tones are speaking most to us. This sectional, like many of the others on this list, can be configured to be left-facing or right-facing depending on your living room setup, and we particularly like that in case you tend to switch up your design layout (we certainly do).

At just 62 inches wide, Sabai’s Essential Loveseat Sectional demonstrates how even the smallest living rooms can accommodate a proper chaise lounge. The compact design features clean lines, a generously sized chaise, and supportive foam cushions, offering the ideal spot to stretch out after a long day. Adding to the sectional’s appeal is its focus on sustainability. It combines a frame made from wood certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)—a third-party verification that ensures ethical wood sourcing—with upholstery fashioned from recycled natural materials. It’s also easy to clean and maintain, largely thanks to its washable slipcovers, sold separately—a welcome feature for anyone whose couch often doubles as a dining chair for meals eaten over the coffee table. Suffice it to say, this sectional is particularly well-suited to apartment living.

CB2’s Deseo sectional brings a little drama to small-space living, courtesy of rich, praline-brown performance velvet, broad arms, and a low-slung silhouette that practically begs you to sink in and stay awhile. The three-piece configuration, matching ottoman, and option for an extra-deep seat only extend the lounging possibilities and allow you to take advantage of every inch of your space. If brown doesn’t fit your space’s palette, worry not; the Deseo comes in plenty of other glamorous colors, including seven other performance velvet upholstery options.

Serious lounging is the goal for Sundays’ Movie Night sectional, with oversized cushions, deep seats, and a relaxed silhouette that makes it difficult to resist the urge to spend the afternoon totally horizontal. The cream linen upholstery adds to its laid-back feel, while the movable ottoman lets you stretch out or create a more open seating arrangement when company comes over. The company’s own LiveLife performance fabric is stain-resistant, moisture-repellent, and washable, with removable slipcovers that make living with a light-colored sofa significantly less intimidating.

Interior Define takes customization very seriously, and the Sloan sectional showcases how having such options can pay off in a small living room. Choose your preferred upholstery, cushion fill, seat depth, and leg style, then fine-tune the dimensions to suit your floor plan. The reversible chaise adds another layer of flexibility, allowing you to change its orientation, in case you rearrange your furniture or move to a new place with a different layout.

Contributor Malia Griggs tested the Sloan in her own 196-square-foot living room, where she found that its supportive cushions, tailored silhouette, and carefully selected dimensions worked beautifully alongside a narrow entryway. “If you enjoy tailoring your décor to your taste, are willing to pay a bit more for quality, and have the patience for a made-to-order process, this is a wonderful sectional—especially for a smaller space,” she added.

What Features Should I Look for in a Sectional for Small Living Rooms?

Modular furniture—any sectional that comes in several parts so you can adjust your sofa to suit the configurations—is built with flexibility in mind, making it the ideal contender for a small living space. We have tested and loved Castlery modular sofas, but a search for modular sectional should give you plenty of other options. A room tight on space can benefit from couches with storage, like those from Albany Park. Now you’ll be able to minimize the clutter and extra blankets by stowing them underneath your seat.

How Do I Arrange a Sectional in a Small Space?

Don’t fall for the tiniest sectional you can find, but rather invest in something well-made—it plays a big part in your living room, after all. While it may seem counterintuitive, Nashville interior designer Amanda Khouri says, “Filling a small room with small furniture can make it feel…well, smaller.”

Designer Alicia Murphy used a sectional in the living room of a teensy trailer she converted into a plush family getaway in Montauk, New York, for this very reason: “If you use a corner sectional rather than a sofa and chair, you most likely will add seating for two or three more people,” Murphy explains, noting that the alternative prevents you from having about 36 inches of dead space in the corner.”

Another way to make it work? Set an L-shaped sectional across from two club chairs to create a conversation zone, advises interior designer Suzanne Dawson.

What Do I Look for in a High-Quality Sectional?

When you’re working with a small space, quality counts. It’s much harder to get away with a mid-century modern knock-off when it’s one of four furniture pieces packed into the room. When shopping for a sectional, evaluate the materials and care instructions. Avoid anything with plywood, and polyester when you can. Seek out solid wood construction, such as walnut, oak, or teak; and premium fabrics, like linen, leather, or chenille. You’ll also want to keep the warranty and return policy in mind, in case you want to send back a piece that doesn’t work for you.

#4843. When Being the Strong One Makes It Hard to Ask for Help

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

There's usually someone in every family, friendship group, or workplace whom people know they can count on. When problems in life arise, that person often gets called to support and fix the issue. Can you relate to being that person?

You have probably heard the advice to take care of yourself before caring for others, or "put your own oxygen mask on first". For a lot of people, being the dependable one becomes central to their identity. But sometimes, being the person everyone counts on comes at the expense of taking care of yourself.

Reliability stops being a habit at some point and becomes who you are. You may start measuring your worth by how much you do for others and how little you need from them. Once that's set, asking for help may feel like breaking character.

That label, "strong one," can ultimately impact your self-image. It may make it more challenging to reach out when you need support. According to a 2025 review of caregiver experiences, participants reported that individuals, due to the pressure to stay strong and reliable, may feel that they are not living up to their role if they seek psychological help.

You may be the person that others call when they need advice or that people turn to when life gets difficult. But when someone asks how you're doing, you change the subject or say “I'm good.”

In a recent 2025 study, experts examined people's beliefs about seeking and receiving help. They found that some people believe accepting help makes them less themselves or threatens their independence. Those beliefs were connected to how people experienced receiving help and to their well-being. Accepting help can be hard, not because support isn't there, but because it can impact how people see themselves.

You're probably used to running things and fixing problems on your own. Letting someone support you means admitting what's actually going on, and that gets uncomfortable when your whole identity is built on being the one who handles everything. To engage in vulnerability, try to ask yourself, "When did I last let myself be vulnerable?" Did it bring relief, or did it leave you reluctant to open up again? Letting someone help sometimes means letting go of control and showing them a side they don't usually see.

It can be even harder when you feel pressure to appear "successful" and seem like you have everything under control. For instance, a recent study introduces another factor that can make asking for help difficult: competition. When employees viewed professional success as a contest, where one person's win meant someone else's loss, they were less likely to seek help from colleagues.

If you always identify as "the strong one", here are a few ways to become more comfortable accepting help:

You don't always have to be the person who has it all together. It's okay to have a bad day, ask someone for help, or admit that you don't know what to do. You spend so much time showing up for others that you sometimes forget you need support too.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Attitudinal barriers to psychological support-seeking among carers of people with a chronic physical health condition: A qualitative meta-synthesis. Patient Education and Counseling, 140, Article 109304. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pec.2025.109304

#4842. The Best Men's Travel Blazers in 2026, Tested by Style Editors

Silhouettes from Uniqlo, Suitsupply, and Eddie Bauer went the distance in our testing.

WHETHER YOU’RE PACKING for a trip or just gearing up for a long commute, keeping a travel blazer in your rotation saves you time—and a lot of outfit stress. When you’re bouncing from one to the next with no time to reset, this is the one piece in your wardrobe that won’t fall apart. Unlike traditional blazers, these travel styles resist wrinkles, breathe easily, and have enough stretch that you still feel comfortable during those cramped flights and shoulder-to-shoulder train rides. On top of that, they’re easy to pack in your luggage and pair with a bunch of ensembles.

Since 2022, we’ve tested over 25 travel blazers, seeing how they hold up in overhead bins, on sweaty commutes, and straight out of a bag. The best ones are tailored, not restrictive, lightweight but not flimsy, and polished without feeling overdone. No one’s traveling in a three-piece suit anymore. Here are the best travel blazers to get you through it all.

In the past year, our style team has tested dozens of travel blazers for functionality and Relwen has it in spades. Right off the bat, we noticed that its cotton-spandex fabric feels super lightweight and comes with enough stretch to let you move beyond limitations. It leans more sport jacket with a four-button design and throat latch that allows you to button all the way up to your neck. There are also functional buttons on the sleeves, which look sharp rolled up. I’ve worn it in low 50s as well as high 70s, and found it to be comfortable in both temps.

Normally, I have to pay to dry clean most of my blazers, but this one can be tossed around my washing machine without falling apart. As for storage, the three exterior patch pockets are similar to any casual blazer, but the large interior pocket has a zip closure with a vertical opening for easy access. It is ideal for stashing valuables.

On top of being a solid choice for away seminars or long flights, this option is great for everyday wear. It looks great during cool evening strolls, dinner dates, and outdoor weddings. Sure, this blazer gets wrinkled easily, but it’s designed to give off a laid-back vibe, as if it’s been worn and broken in over time.

In Rhone’s vast assortment, the brand carries a travel blazer with a killer slim cut. It has a sporty vibe, but looks clean enough for meetings that aren’t too formal. The Flex-Knit fabric is breathable and moisture-wicking, which means you stay cool and the garment doesn’t become damp or develop unpleasant odors from sweat. The polyester material has plenty of stretch, so I never felt any restriction in the arm area when I grabbed my coffee or reached up to the high cabinet.

I’ve paired it with everything from a basic tee to an oxford shirt, and it looks great with just about anything in your wardrobe—a true testament to its versatility. Plus, the material is ultra-light, making it a comfortable pick to throw on. Unlike Relwen’s travel blazer, this one can’t go in the washer—you have to take a trip to the dry cleaners.

Eddie Bauer’s travel blazer is practically indestructible. The fabric is hardcore and can take a beating, thanks to the reinforced seams and durable water-repellent finish. The latter especially makes sure you’re covered if you spill a drink or get caught in a downpour. And when you’re commuting, you can secure your passport or phone inside zippered compartments.

During our testing, we found that the two-way stretch made a journey a breeze, giving us the freedom to move through busy airports and crowded streets. Plus, the universal fit hits the sweet spot, so it’s comfortable for all body types without being too tight or too loose.

Although Uniqlo’s design looks like a wool blazer replica, it’s one of the most breathable styles I’ve ever worn. It’s made with the brand’s proprietary AirSense fabric, a lightweight polyester material that dries in minutes and keeps me cool. Typically, when I wear a traditional blazer in the summertime and in the muggy subway, I sweat like a dog. But when I wore this one in 80-degree weather to a work brunch, I was comfortable and dry the whole time. It’s relaxed enough to wear with chinos or jeans, but still has a dressy vibe that can pull off a full-suit look with trousers.

I found it’s not too fitted in the waist, which lets me layer shirts or knits easier in the cooler temps. There’s no bunching to where I feel stuffed. You can snag it in the typical neutral colors like gray and navy, perfect for the office followed by dinner plans. Like Relwen’s offering, this one is machine washable, but I recommend turning it inside out in a mesh bag. On the other hand, it’s way more structured with a natural shaping in the shoulders and sleeves. And yeah, it’s the most affordable option on this list, clocking in under $100, but it doesn’t look or feel like a budget buy. You’re getting the same premium quality that you’d get with a blazer that cost a few hundred bucks.

The front pockets are deep enough to carry your earbuds or wallet, so either won’t fall out as you’re maneuvering through the airport. Whether you’re packing it all in a backpack or suitcase, it’s a breeze to toss in and hit the road. Plus, we found no signs of wrinkles after unloading our clothes in the hotel.

Unlike stiff travel blazers that we’ve tested, this one bends and moves with you, so it doesn’t feel like you’re stuck in a straightjacket. The slimmer cut is perfect for guys who have an athletic or lean build, as it accentuates a trim silhouette and creates a sharp appearance. It’s a perfect match with a pair of summer pants, but looks just as cool with jeans and a tee.

When you want to look like you mean business at client dinners or conferences, you should reach for this blazer from Hugo Boss. Most travel blazers prioritize comfort at the expense of polish, but this one manages to deliver both. Our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan loves how sharp this slim-fit silhouette looks on him. He says it's tailored without feeling restrictive, while the stretch-infused, polyester-wool fabric gives you enough mobility for long flights and days spent hauling luggage through airports. The biggest differentiator, though, is right in the name: it’s washable. I can wear it repeatedly on a multi-day trip, freshen it up without a costly dry-cleaning bill, and pack it with far less anxiety than a traditional wool sport coat.

I wore the jacket on a full travel day that included a flight, a lengthy commute, and several hours seated at meetings. It kept its shape surprisingly well, resisting the creases and rumpling that typically throw off more formal tailoring after being folded inside a carry-on. What impressed me most was how effortlessly it transitioned from travel wear to evening attire. I could step off a plane and head directly to a dinner reservation without feeling underdressed. Admittedly, the jacket isn’t as soft or unstructured as more casual travel blazers from performance-focused brands. Also, the slimmer cut may feel less forgiving if you prefer a relaxed fit. But if your priority is maintaining a clean, business-ready vibe while still getting travel-friendly performance, I haven’t found many options that strike the balance as well as this one.

If you’re looking for a travel blazer that leans more dressy with European tailoring and luxurious quality for a great price point, Suitsupply is your best bet. Instead of a boxy, rigid silhouette that’s on trend right now, this timeless design has a natural shoulder, single-breasted closure, and a half-canvas construction that helps the jacket mold to your body over time while maintaining a solid drape.

It’s made with medium weight pure wool, but I wasn’t burning up wearing it with a tank top at a rooftop party. The cut is relaxed through the chest and waist, with a clean, structured drape that follows the body without pulling. I have to admit, it does wrinkle quite a bit when I’m sitting down for a long amount of time. If I’m traveling somewhere warm and still want to look put-together, Buck Mason’s carry-on blazer is the one I keep coming back to.
