#4721. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4720. The 8 Best Electric Razors for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Editor

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHOEVER SAID PATIENCE is a virtue did not have facial hair, or at least, they weren’t regularly shaving it. Even as Men’s Health’s Grooming Editor, I’m usually running behind and rushing through my shave routine, whether I’m packing my traveling grooming essentials, deciding what toiletries to bring camping, or just trying to get to work. If it weren’t for electric razors, I would have committed to a life of looking like Charles Darwin long ago.

Of course, there are plenty of reasons punctual guys might want to use an electric razor in lieu of traditional cartridge razors. These shavers are gentler on skin, gliding across the face with less direct blade contact to reduce irritation and minimize the risk of nicks and cuts. They also help prevent razor bumps and burns by trimming hair above the surface instead of dragging against the skin like traditional razors do.

To be clear, it takes skin a few sessions to get used to shaving with these devices if you’ve been a long-time cartridge devotee. This is because electric razors move differently and do not cut as close, so your skin needs time to adapt to the new sensation and technique. Also, switching razors changes how the blades interact with your skin, which can cause temporary irritation as your skin builds tolerance.

Still, these tools streamline the whole process: they're fast, easy to use, and travel-friendly since you don’t need to pack extra products, like shaving cream. Many models even come with smart features like pressure sensors and AI, making them more intuitive and unique to the user. Most you can use wet or dry, with or without shaving cream, and they're versatile enough for your face, head, or body. Plus, some have add-ons that can help you replace multiple grooming tools, simplify your routine, and free up space on your bathroom shelf.

But regardless of why you’re using an electric razor, the biggest thing is finding the right one for you. The good news is that no matter what your budget, skin or hair type, or grooming acumen, there's an electric razor that will suit your needs.

Braun electric razors have been a favorite of Men’s Health since we first launched our grooming vertical in 2018. For years, we maintained that the Braun Series 9 Pro was in a class of its own when it came to electric shavers. Then, the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus was released, which took these tools to an entirely new level.

At first glance, the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus looks almost identical to the original Series 9—and that’s not a bad thing. It keeps the same ergonomic design, which strikes a near-perfect balance in the hand: lightweight enough to maneuver easily, yet hefty enough to feel secure while shaving. Like its predecessor, the Pro Plus features five cutting elements that trim hairs down to an ultra-smooth 0.05 mm, giving you that just-shaved feel with impressive precision that’s as close as you’ll get without using an old-school barbershop blade.

Where it really starts to separate itself from the previous model, and any other electric razor for that matter, is the blades. The OG version’s blades were titanium, but the Pro Plus blades are made from surgical-grade stainless steel that stay sharper, allowing for a more effective shave that lasts longer. The Braun Series 9 Pro Plus, like the original version, features an ultra-thin ProLift blade (which looks like a gold bar on the razor head itself) that helps to lift hair away from your skin for a thorough cut.

What Else to Consider: Despite all that praise, the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus doesn’t lead the pack in terms of raw motor speed. It clocks in at 40,000 cutting actions per minute, which is solid but far from the top. But similar to Draymond Green’s career stats, the numbers don’t tell the whole story—this delivers the most powerful shave on the market. Sure, the Philips Norelco Shaver 9800 boasts a much faster motor (up to 150,000-cuts-per-minute), but speed isn’t everything.

What sets the Series 9 Pro Plus apart is Braun’s Sonic Technology, which adds 10,000 micro-vibrations per minute on top of the motor's output. These vibrations help lift and capture more hair with each pass, making every stroke more effective and efficient. The razor also features a pop-up trimmer and a flexing head, which performed especially well compared to the Panasonic Arc5.

Its pivoting head perfectly hugs facial contours with more precision, likely due to its slightly smaller, more agile design. It also includes the AI-driven ProSensoAdapt, which senses beard density 300 times per second, according to the brand. This automatically adjusts power in real time for a smoother, more personalized shave.

Why We Chose It: Shaving with the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus rarely takes more than five minutes, even less when my stubble is light, but its standout feature is the incredibly close shave it delivers. The innovative focus is on lifting hairs more effectively from the skin to ensure a smoother finish.

Another feature I didn’t know I needed from an electric razor is the ProComfort pre-shave head, which gently lifts and prepares hairs for a closer, more comfortable shave. It does this by using fine, vibrating blades to raise and align hairs before the main shaver cuts them.

These upgrades make a real difference. It’s by far the closest shave I get from an electric razor, especially when I use the ProComfort head beforehand to prep my skin. No other tool gets me this close to 5 o'clock before the shadow shows up.

Long-Term Results: I’ve been using my Braun Series 9 Pro Plus for over a year, and it still shaves just as well today as it did right out of the box. Overall performance has not changed, though there has been a slight decline in cutting power when the blade dulled. But replacing the head was easy and brought the shaver back to business immediately.

Another Men’s Health shaving staple, especially for those with sensitive skin. You’d expect a razor this powerful to cause irritation, especially considering its five (incredibly sharp) blades, but it doesn’t. The Arc5 shaves nearly as close as any manual razor and cream combo I’ve used, and the pivoting head effortlessly glides over tricky areas like my neck and jawline without missing a spot.

Despite its impressive performance, the device feels light in the hand and operates super quietly; it’s barely loud enough for you to realize it’s on. While it doesn’t match the Braun Series 9’s extras like AI-powered shave sensors that adjust to beard density, I’ve still found this simpler version more than capable. It gives a clean, close shave without any fuss.

What Else to Consider: With a wide head and a strong motor, this shaver is powerful. It boasts 55,000-cuts-per-minute—more than the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus but less than the absurd Norelco 9800 150,000-cuts-per-minute motor. Even if you don’t have sensitive skin, go easy until you get the hang of how much to press the foil against your face.

Like Davante Adams in the middle of the field, the Arc5 cuts fast. Still, don’t rush through shave jobs, as this can cause some irritation if you’re not careful, no matter the device you’re using. Once you get the hang of it, though, it minimizes the amount of time you have to shave the same area. Overall, it is slightly bulkier than the closest similar razor (Braun Series 9) and has a shorter battery life (45 minutes versus 60 minutes), which could come down to the fact that it’s just a larger device in general.

The Panasonic Arc5’s blades are hypoallergenic, as they’re made from surgical-grade stainless steel that resists corrosion, minimizes skin reactions, and maintains a smooth, low-friction surface, all of which makes it ideal for dealing with sensitive skin. Additionally, the foils covering the blades are designed to be gentle and smooth, which further helps protect the skin from irritation or razor burn.

Why We Chose It: In addition to convenience, the biggest draw of electric razors is that they’re much gentler on skin, helping avoid the razor bumps and irritation that come with close manual shaves. What stands out to me about this model is how closely it shaves—nearly as close as a traditional wet razor, yet without the usual irritation.

After the few shaves it took for my skin to adapt, I noticed a significant drop in bumps. It’s a powerful, efficient tool that’s straightforward and intuitive with no unnecessary features to complicate things. For anyone with sensitive skin, this razor is easily the most skin-friendly option I’ve tried, and it delivers smooth results without the harsh aftermath.

Long-Term Results: The Arc5 holds up over time. After months of use, the cutting power has not decreased a bit, and post-shave irritation remains a rare occurrence. The blades are as sharp and gentle as they were out of the box.

For anyone constantly battling stubborn neck hairs, this is the razor for you. The Norelco 9800 brings AI into the shaving routine to deliver an impressively close and precise shave. Its rotary heads easily follow facial contours, while built-in pressure sensors give real-time feedback, letting you know when they’re applying too much or too little pressure.

Powered by Dual Steel Precision blades, which are two layers of self‑sharpening stainless steel blades that increase cutting speed and efficiency, making up to 150,000 cuts per minute. This razor doesn’t leave a single stray hair behind.

With 72 rotating blades offering full 360-degree movement, it seamlessly adapts to every curve of the face. To top it off, the smart companion app tracks shaving patterns and offers personalized tips for better technique, making this one of the most advanced grooming tools on the market.

What Else to Consider: The Norelco 9800 blows every other rotary shaver out of the water. Not only is the motor by far the most powerful (again, 150,000-cuts-per-minute!), but the three-head design offers a great range of motion, allowing for more pivoting and a closer shave around the contours of your face. The blades on the 9800 also have a micro-bead coating to help reduce irritation, which we found helpful.

Though not usually a huge tech junkie, I recommend using the app to change the settings, especially if you use it wet or dry, because adjusting those settings manually can be difficult. That being said, it does take a bit of time to adjust to your style of shaving. It’s a bit overly responsive at first, so when you first apply more pressure in less sensitive areas, like your cheeks, it can overcompensate when moving to areas like the curves in your neck and lead to nicks. However, it quickly adjusted after a couple of uses.

Why We Chose It: If it's features you want, this electric razor is chock-full of them. AI helps guide your shaving to create the best shave you can possibly get, as long as you use those features to their full advantage. If you don’t, you’ll still get a good, close shave, but this thing really sings when everything works together. Similar to Braun’s AI, the 9800 senses hair density and automatically adjusts; however, it also provides real-time pressure feedback via the light ring and connected app.

Long-Term Results: This definitely proved to be for the type of guy who likes to tinker and customize, and I can appreciate that. Of all the rotary-head razors I’ve tested, this one flexed and pivoted to the shape of my face the best without missing too many spots. Furthermore, the cleaning and charging station is the sleekest and simplest on the market, and I always appreciate space-saving.

My favorite thing about the Chairman Plus is how streamlined the design is. Sure, there are a handful of nifty gadgets and features, like the travel lock, SkinSafe blade protection, and ergonomic grip, but none are excessive. More than anything, however, they’re all functional.

So often with grooming devices, they tend to sound exciting or interesting, but when put into practice, they’re either overly complicated or straight-up unnecessary. That’s not the case with The Chairman Plus, as every feature was clearly designed to simplify the shaving experience and make it as easy as possible.

What Else to Consider: Of all the practical design boons of this trimmer, the most notable is also the simplest: its grip. Thanks to an innovative (albeit uncomplicated) ergonomic design, this shaver is the easiest to hold and use on this list. Contrary to the Chairman Pro's more straight horizontal handle, the Plus features a slight indent on each side under the razor head to create more of a T-shape than the traditional V-shape.

I have been known to drop razors mid-job from time to time, so I found this a welcome update that creates a much easier-to-hold grip. It’s ideal for clumsy people like me or those new to electric shavers in general.

Why We Chose It: Ultimately, this selection came down to how easy this razor is to use, along with how gentle it is on skin. If you’re new to electric razors or shaving in general, the Chairman Plus represents a low-risk introduction to these tools. At barely over a pound, it’s super lightweight, and its SkinSafe-protected blades, which feature a built-in safety guard between sets of rounded (rather than harsher straight ones) stainless steel blades, make cuts and tugs few and far between. While the shave isn’t as close as other options on this list, sans the OneBlade, it’s one of the more gentle and certainly the best for beginners.

Long-Term Results: I really dig the travel lock on this device; it’s simple to use, but also takes some effort to click on and off. This helped me avoid accidentally turning it on when traveling and slicing through other products or ruining clothes packed near it (did I mention the clumsiness?). Again, it doesn’t give the closest shave, but that’s not always the most important thing if you have sensitive skin, like I do, and would rather avoid irritation (which this does).

If you’re looking for the closest trim without completely shaving your beard (like a slight five-o’clock shadow), this easy-to-use electric shaver is a top choice. As someone who was once deeply committed to old-school blades, I appreciate how this handles like a traditional razor, thanks to an ergonomic design and classically shaped handle, but you can’t treat it exactly the same as your typical razor.

The razor and the other features may be basic, but they’re effective. It’s user-friendly and intuitive to use with a minimal learning curve, which to me is always a plus. Long-Term Results: After using the Lawnmower 5.0 for a year, it’s still my go-to for body grooming, especially sensitive areas down below. If I based this list on purely shaving capabilities without any consideration for price or portability, Braun Nevo would probably be my top pick. Why We Chose It: Only one electric razor can match the Nevo's shaving performance, and it's my best overall pick on this list. If you can swing that price tag, however, you’ll struggle to shave with most other electric razors after experiencing this one.

The blade type is a key factor to consider when choosing an electric razor. You’ll typically choose between two main options: rotary blades and foil blades.

If you usually let your stubble grow out or don’t shave every day, a rotary electric razor is your best bet. Its circular motion and flexible head follow the curves of your face, helping it cut through longer or more uneven hair with ease. Rotary razors work especially well for those with normal to tougher skin and medium to coarse beard density, offering a comfortable and efficient shave even after a few days of growth.

A foil works best for shorter facial hair or when you're aiming for a close shave similar to classic razors. It uses oscillating blades hidden beneath a thin, perforated foil that captures and cuts hairs as they emerge through the mesh. While a foil shaver tends to be noisier than rotary models, it offers deeper precision. To get the smoothest results, use it with straight, steady strokes—moving back and forth along the face and neck. This design makes foil razors ideal for those who shave daily or want clean, sharp lines around facial hair.

Corded razors plug directly into a power source, so you don’t have to worry about charging or replacing batteries. As a result, they deliver more consistent power and longer performance. Since they don’t need to conserve energy, they also usually run stronger than cordless models. That said, cordless razors offer added convenience, especially for travel or grooming on the go, with options powered by either rechargeable or disposable batteries. Ultimately, the right choice depends on your routine and how much flexibility you need.

Many premium models offer additional features or accessories to enhance the shave experience or make it more convenient, including:

The Men’s Health grooming team has been extensively testing electric razors since 2018. For years, we’ve been putting shavers to the test, evaluating their effectiveness, durability, and ease of use over long periods of time. As someone who can get a five o'clock shadow before lunch, I am constantly shaving. This has given me a consistent canvas to test and retest editor favorites, as well as the latest innovations and new grooming releases.

For this story, I considered the team’s reviews and notes of top-performing razors dating back eight years, in addition to my own experience, to land on 15 options to extensively test or retest over an 18-month trial period. I’ve also included before-and-after shots of yours truly for most of the razors to show the kind of shave each one delivers. Based on this first-hand use, I narrowed that list to eight, representing the best electric razors for men to buy in 2026.

Both electric and manual razors use blades to cut hair, but they do it in different ways. Manual razors pull each hair up with the first blade, then slice it closer to the skin with the following blades—kind of like using a knife. Electric razors, on the other hand, work more like scissors. Most use a foil system: hair enters tiny holes in the foil, and internal blades cut it from beneath. Rotary versions use a slightly different mechanism, but the concept is similar.

Manual razors shave closer because the blades touch the skin directly. That closeness comes with a downside: higher chances of razor burn, bumps, or ingrown hairs, especially if you skip proper prep or use a dull blade. Electric razors always have a barrier between the blade and skin, so while they won’t shave quite as close, they’re often gentler and better suited for sensitive skin.

Using an electric razor is much easier to pick up compared to a traditional or safety razor. Still, don’t just grab yours and start shaving right away. Take the time to learn how to get the closest shave possible before speeding through the process for the best results.

Start your shave with clean skin. Whether you’re using a wet or dry shaver, you should tackle your scruff right after washing your face. For dry shavers, apply a small amount of pre-shave oil or wash your face and then gently pat it dry. These shavers perform best when the stubble is firm and completely dry.

Keep the razor at a 90-degree angle to your skin to avoid cutting hairs unevenly. There’s no need to press hard, as a light grip does the job. Pressing down too much, especially around the jaw or chin, can lead to patchy results and irritation. With a foil shaver, I stick to back-and-forth strokes. If I’m using a rotary, I’ll go with either circular or straight motions, depending on what feels best.

Reading the manual might seem unnecessary (and boring), but brands often include specific tips or techniques tailored to their design. Those little details can make a big difference, resulting in a noticeably smoother shave. It might not be Hemingway, but taking a few minutes to go through the instructions usually pays off in better results and a more comfortable experience overall.

As long as I stick to proper maintenance and care, I get a consistently smooth shave from electric razors. If you’re new to these tools, however, give your skin about two weeks to adjust—it makes a big difference. A little patience and upkeep go a long way.

One of the first things I check in an electric razor is how easy it is to clean because this will help both its effectiveness and longevity (not to mention my blood pressure). Skipping regular cleaning can clog the blades with hair and gunk, which not only affects performance but also shortens the razor’s life. When using a waterproof device, I always rinse mine under running water after each use, then use a small brush to clear out any buildup on the foil.

That foil is key to getting a smooth, even shave, but it’s delicate. If it gets bent or damaged, replace it right away. Letting it go risks rough shaves, irritation, or even breakouts from dragging dirt across your skin. Some higher-end models, like the Braun Series 9, come with automatic cleaning stations. They’re super convenient (even if a bit bulky and noisy) and use replaceable cartridges that last around three months—about $5 each in a multi-pack. While not essential, they definitely make it easier to stay on top of maintenance.

Read More: How To Maintain Your Beard Trimmer

High-quality electric razors—especially those in the $200-plus range—can last years, sometimes even five or more if well maintained. To keep mine running strong, I make sure to replace the blades and foil regularly. Depending on the brand, blade replacement is usually recommended every 6 to 18 months. I also keep an eye on the foil. If it gets dented or damaged, I swap it out immediately since most replacement cartridges include both parts.

These typically cost between $20 and $50. Battery life is typically the first thing to go. Over time, even the best razors start to lose their charge faster or run with less power. When I notice my shave isn’t as close, or the razor starts pulling instead of cutting cleanly, that’s my cue that it might be time for a new one.

November through New Year’s is marketed as the magical season, and for many people, it can be. But if you are struggling with infertility and/or pregnancy loss, it can represent two months of triggers, traumas, jealousy, and misery. Why? Lots of reasons.

Many people save surprise pregnancy announcements for gatherings, which can be agonizing for anyone who wants nothing more than to make such an announcement themselves. Family and friend parties bring forced encounters. Intrusive questions are common: So when are you going to start a family? I hear you’ve been struggling. I think you should see my cousin’s doctor. You need to gain weight, exercise less, try my herbalist, or just adopt.

And it doesn't help when the focus of TV specials, commercials, and religious services is on babies and children. What can you do to make this season a bit less dread-worthy? Maybe even experience some joy?

Don’t assume that every pregnancy announcement or belly was achieved easily or through spontaneous sex (roughly 1 in every 37 babies are conceived through IVF). Many people never share their infertility struggles, and most of those who build their families through donor eggs, sperm, or embryo don’t tell anyone.

You are not alone. It is estimated that 1 in 6 individuals struggle with family-building.

If you can’t get into the holiday mood whatsoever, don’t pressure yourself. The majority of those experiencing infertility report symptoms of anxiety and depression, and women experience the same level of psychological distress as do women facing cancer or heart disease.

Most importantly, put yourself on your own list; nurture yourself.

Resolve is the National Infertility Organization. They provide patient education and support in every state.

Prelude patients also have access to emotional support information/resources on their patient portal.

ASRM is the American Society for Reproductive Medicine. They provide up-to-date, accurate medical information.

#4717. Tesla Cybertruck had its best month in over a year. It’s still going away

New EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.

Across all new vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.

EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October. That’s up from 10.3% a year earlier and well above October’s industrywide average of 6.8%.

Tesla’s average selling price fell from September to $54,194, but it was still up 1.2% year over year. The Cybertruck helped push that average higher. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 1,914 Cybertrucks in October, its best month in more than a year, at an average price of $92,380.

The sad thing is that there likely is a market for an affordable electric pickup truck in the U.S. to compete with Ford’s F150 and others. The Ford Fathom may be the best fit for that market, now.

That sales bump comes as Tesla prepares to end Cybertruck production at its Austin factory in mid-2027. Elon Musk said Tesla will dismantle the assembly line around June or July to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis.

#4716. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4715. Feeling the Pain of Others

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

“Are you sure your work hasn’t gotten to you?” he asked. We were visiting our family in the Caribbean. We had hiked to the top of the cliffs on a small island, and for a moment the entire family stood quietly together, marveling at the sea. It was an exquisite sight—turquoise water as far as you could see, and a vast, cloudless sky. As we reached the edge of the cliffs, my first thought was, This is unbelievably beautiful. My second thought was, I wonder how many people have killed themselves by jumping off these cliffs.

I assumed everyone thought this; I asked my question out loud. My stepfather-in-law turned to me slowly and asked his question with such sincerity that I finally understood: My work had gotten to me. I didn’t even tell him the rest of my thoughts: Where would the helicopter land? Could it land on the beach, or would it land on this cliff and then they’d belay down? Is there even a Level 1 trauma center in the Caribbean? Would they have to go to Miami? Would they stop you in customs? It was quite a list.

I had always considered myself self-aware, but this was the first time I saw my work had transformed my engagement with the world.

My jobs had brought me into intimate contact with people who were living close to or experiencing different types of acute trauma. I worked in confidential locations and at large institutions. I worked days, evenings, and graveyard shifts. I worked in local communities, throughout the country, and the world.

Over time, friends, family, and even clients said I needed a vacation. Otherwise, stop taking everything so seriously. But I could not hear them; I was doing God’s work. They could either step up and help me or step off. I did not need to reflect on myself. I was arrogant, self-righteous, and impassioned, perhaps to the point of selective blindness. I was convinced that I was just fine.

After so many stories of abuse, death, and tragedies, including missing children, deported loved ones, climate disasters, and other nightmares, I had absorbed and accumulated other people’s pain to the point that it had become part of me, and my view of the world had changed. But I finally understood that this exposure to other people’s overwhelm had fundamentally changed me. I did the work for a long time with little ability to integrate my experiences emotionally, cognitively, physically, or spiritually. I suffered from compassion fatigue.

Rather than staying in touch with the heart that was breaking, I started building walls. In my case, this meant I became increasingly cocky. I had no access to humility, which we all need when honestly engaging our own internal process. Rather than acknowledge my own pain and helplessness in the face of things I could not control, I raged at the possible external causes. I sharpened my critique of systems and society. I became more dogmatic, opinionated, and intolerant of other people’s views. It never occurred to me that my anger might in part be functioning as a shield or that I was warding off anguish. A widely held belief: If you’re tough enough, cool enough, and committed enough, you’ll keep on keeping on. You’ll suck it up.

Instead, I began the long haul of making change. I acknowledged the effects of other people’s pain; I made room for my own internal process. Over the years, I gradually let go. This fatigue takes a personal and professional toll.

We are slow to recognize such fatigue as a broad social concern rather than an isolated individual issue—through a job, daily life, or caregiving. It also goes beyond exposure to human suffering; other species and the planet are also in pain.

I needed a new framework that allowed me to bear witness to suffering without surrendering my ability to live fully—I call the concept trauma stewardship. This refers to the entire conversation: How we are affected over time, how we make sense of, learn from, and ultimately transform, individually and collectively.

In stewardship, we are entrusted with people’s stories and lives, animals’ well-being, and our planet’s health. We understand that this is an honor as well as a responsibility. As stewards, we make room for and honor others’ hardship and suffering, yet we do not assume their pain as our own.

The essayist E. B. White once wrote that the early American author, naturalist, and philosopher Henry Thoreau had perhaps been “torn by two powerful and opposing drives—the desire to enjoy the world, and the urge to set the world straight.”

#4714. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4713. Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the company’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

Napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He said that at the start of Q3, the company had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”

He said Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.

Lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory.

So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.

In Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806, down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.

Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.

By Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.

Elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he said Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also launched door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.

It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk said Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers. Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.

Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.

When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.

About a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the company preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.

It worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.

We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO said that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.

I like to think people were relatively patient with Tesla's growing pains when Model 3 was ramping up in 2018, largely because there weren't many alternatives for a sporty, relatively affordable EV.

But it's 2026. Buyers have plenty of options now, and the patience that early EV adopters once had for these kinds of mistakes is long gone.

This is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.

But it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.

Tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.

#4712. Talking to Youth About Online Gambling and Sports Betting

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

The gambling landscape has changed dramatically over a short period of time. Prediction markets (with a minimum age of 18), sports betting (complete with micro-bets), fantasy sports betting, iCasinos, and gambling activities within video games make gambling more accessible and more convenient than ever before. Indeed, online gambling “allows continuous and immediate access to gambling from virtually anywhere” (Forrest et al., 2026).

Adolescents have likely been exposed to online gambling in more ways than their parents might expect. Therefore, it is important for parents/caregivers to broach this topic to dispel myths about gambling, present accurate information about potential risks, and offer guidance. For parents who are unfamiliar with the online gambling landscape, here is a quick overview:

Parents can find ways to bring up online gambling and sports betting with youth by referencing something they read online (like this blog post!) or after watching a commercial for a gambling app on TV. A few example questions parents could ask include:

Once the conversation has begun, it is important for parents to listen with curiosity and care. Rather than using fear tactics, parents can provide accurate information about online gambling and sports betting to help adolescents understand the potential risks. It may be helpful to share essential facts:

Importantly, the goal is to facilitate a dialogue with youth, rather than having a one-way conversation. Parents can draw their adolescent into the conversation by asking: Why do they believe people are drawn to online gambling and sports betting? What are some myths they have heard about gambling? In what ways are gambling operators trying to make their products as enticing as possible? What might they do if a friend discloses that they have gotten into some trouble with gambling?

Finally, it is always helpful for parents to ask adolescents about their goals, short-term and long-term (e.g., what are their professional goals? Health-related goals? Financial goals? Spiritual goals?) and to explore their values. In this way, youth can recognize the discrepancy between their goals/values and gambling behaviors, and this recognition can serve as motivation not to engage (Miller & Rollnick, 2023).

Parents may be hesitant to start this conversation with their adolescent due to the fear they won’t have all the answers or may not say all the “right things.” Yet, the goal is not for parents to use the perfect words; instead, the goal is to open the lines of communication to encourage ongoing conversations with adolescents about the risk behaviors they face today. Saying the right thing is less important than showing adolescents they care about their experiences and are available to talk and listen.

#4711. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4710. Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:00 PM EST

Today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes. Prehistoric cultures unfortunately didn’t have this luxury, and often responded dramatically to such changes. In northern Peru, archaeological evidence indicates local societies sometimes even turned to mass human sacrifices in an attempt to stop destructive flooding from events like El Niño.

That said, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate issues. According to their study recently published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, such brutal moments were actually pretty rare occurrences in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley.

“The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” said New York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.

The Lambayeque Valley is located inside northern Peru’s coastal desert, but the region has hosted residents for  6,000 years. Although the valley generally receives little rainfall, its rivers and proximity to the sea allowed communities to flourish there for generations, including societies like the Moche from roughly 100–750 CE, and the Sicán from about 750–1375 CE.

“Archaeological evidence shows that in so many ways they were mirrors of us—in how they lived their daily lives, interacted with their world, ran their economies, and confronted (and sometimes contributed to) environmental crises,” explained George Mason University archaeologist and study co-author Haagen Klaus.

Previous excavations have indicated that mass human sacrifices possibly preceded the collapse of the Moche and Sicán’s political systems. Researchers have since hypothesized that these acts likely coincided with periods of mass flooding,probably due to El Niño weather oscillations. Just like today, these weather events destroyed food stocks and disrupted agricultural production. Since large human sacrificial rituals may have been attempts by the ruling class to restore balance to nature, the team to wonder if violence was simply a more common facet of everyday life for the Moche and Sicán.

“If these big ritual sacrifices were indicative of some underlying crisis, we hypothesized that these events might have been extending into people’s everyday experience of the world,” said Snyder.

Klaus, Snyder, and their collaborators turned to the Lambayeque Valley Biohistory Project’s skeletal archive for answers. The collection spans about 3,000 years of history across 30 different archaeological sites. The team established relatively precise death estimates for over 1,600 individuals, while also examining them for evidence of intentional cranial trauma associated with human sacrifice. Contrary to their theory, only 25 remains (1.6 percent of the sample pool) showed signs of violence, while just 77 displayed indicators of accidental trauma. Of those, none were directly linked to known periods of past ecological crises.

“In Lambayeque, there’s 6,000 years of creative adaptations to El Niño and longer-term changes in climate, and widespread violence wasn’t one of them,” concluded Klaus.

The study’s authors noted that because they were notable to radiocarbon date all of the remains, their findings remain broader estimates of wide time periods. At the same time, they stressed the evidence underscores humanity’s history of facing intense climate challenges not with violence, but adaptation.

“This really highlights that widespread violence isn’t a predetermined response to climate change,” said Snyder. “As a society, we both get to and have to choose how we respond to our own climate crisis.”

“Violence and social unraveling are not destined outcomes, ever,” added Klaus.

#4709. Kia launches two new PV5 electric van variants in the UK

Kia opened orders for two new PV5 electric van variants, the PV5 Chassis and PV5 Cargo L2/H2, in the UK.

The PV5 is Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business. Built on Hyundai Motor’s dedicated modular skateboard platform, E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to enable “limitless possibilities.”

So far, the PV5 has mostly been available in Passenger and Cargo body styles with several different variations.

Kia added the PV5 Chassis, an open-bed model that can be converted into just about anything. In the UK, Kia is offering conversions through TGS Automotive Group, including lightweight tipper, Dropside, and Box solutions.

The PV5 Chassis is available exclusively with the long-range 71.2 kWh battery in the UK, which Kia said could offer a potential WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km).

For reference, the PV5 Cargo L2/H1, which uses the same 71.2 kWh battery, offers a WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km). Other markets will also have a standard-range 51.1 kWh option.

The Chassis model is 4,610 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,935 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.

Its compact size and 5.5-meter turning radius, Kia said, make it easy to maneuver in city streets, construction sites, and other tight work areas.

Inside, the PV5 Chassis features two seats. Like other variants, it includes a 12.9″ navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The Chassis model supports DC fast charging up to 120 kW, enabling the battery to charge from 10% to 80% in about 30 minutes. Using an 11 kW AC supply, it takes about 6 hours and 30 minutes to charge from 10% to 100%.

Payload depends on the configuration. Kia said the Dropside offers a payload of up to 633 kg, while the Tipper can carry 561 kg.

In the UK, the PV5 Chassis is now on sale from £32,916 ($43,400) on the road, including the expected £5,000 ($6,700) UK Zero Emission Van Grant.

However, it’s an “incomplete vehicle,” as Kia describes it. The converted PV5 Dropside is priced from £40,110 ($53,500) on the road, including the ZEVG, while the PV5 Tipper starts at £41,310 ($55,000).

Kia also launched the larger PV5 Cargo L2/H2 in the UK. The new variant is 4,695mm long, 1,895mm wide, and 2,200mm high, with a 2,995mm wheelbase.

The taller roof opens up an internal cargo-area height of 1,815mm. It also offers a greater load capacity than the L1/H1 and L2/H2, with 5.2 cubic meters.

It’s available in three- and four-door configurations with the choice of two or three seats. The three-door versions have a maximum payload of 630 kg, while the four-door models have dual sliding doors and offer a payload of up to 600 kg. Both versions can tow up to 1,500 kg.

Like the Chassis model, the PV5 Cargo L2/H2 is available in the UK exclusively with the 71.2 kWh battery, which provides a WLTP range of up to 239 miles.

Inside, it features the same setup as the other PV5 variants, including a 12.9″ touchscreen navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display.

The base PV5 Cargo L2/H2 Essential two-seat starts at £35,016 ($46,700), on the road, including ZEVG.

#4708. Worried About Your Drinking? How to Cut Down, Comfortably

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

How is your relationship with alcohol? Do you feel like you drink too much, perhaps vowing to cut down but slipping back into uncomfortable but familiar patterns? Many of us do. And that's hard, because alcohol is a socially acceptable drug, especially in Western societies. In the UK, you can buy it in supermarkets, grocery shops on every corner, in pubs, restaurants, and cafés. If you go to a party, alcohol is served. Or at dinner, people keep topping up your glass.

Alcohol is ubiquitous and hard to consume healthily, even with the best of intentions. Even if you're not alcohol-dependent, you may be uncomfortable about the amount you consume, but feel powerless to change that. Unfortunately, numerous studies show that regular drinking can have a major impact on your health, contributing to diseases including cancer, cardiovascular disease, dementia, and gastrointestinal diseases. It's clear that, in an ideal world, sobriety is the healthiest choice we can make. And if you do enjoy a glass of wine or beer, drinking in moderation is the next best option.

If you would like to cut down, the first step is to understand why you drink too much. Let's start with the fact that alcohol tastes and feels good. If you've had a long day, a glass or two of wine helps you relax, gives you a warm, fuzzy feeling, and helps you transition from work to downtime. These transitions can be tricky for us, and we may use substances to help—for example, the morning coffee that provides the energy boost we need to transition from sleepiness to an alert, ready-to-work mode.

So, like other oft-consumed substances, alcohol feels good and helps us transition from one state to another. Another factor in our alcohol consumption is peer pressure. In my country, this starts as a teenager, when friends encourage you to drink excessively to be "cool" or "fun." This pressure continues at university, where heavy drinking is often socially sanctioned and encouraged.

Even in middle age and later years, having a beer in pubs or half a bottle of wine with dinner is seen as normal and desirable. Opting not to drink, although more and more common, can be tricky if your friends are on the boozier side. Although sobriety is increasingly embraced by the younger generation, people of my age (approaching 60) have grown up with alcohol, and opting for sobriety, or occasional drinking, is an effortful, often socially frowned-upon choice.

Viewed through an internal family systems (IFS) lens, there is another pressure to drink, coming from inside your head. In IFS, drinking to excess, or in any way compulsively, is due to the actions of a protective part known as a "firefighter." This part's sole purpose is to extinguish the flames of pain that another—young, vulnerable—part might be struggling with. Firefighters are reactive and impulsive and have no sense of consequences—if you drink a whole bottle of wine, you may feel awful in the morning, but if it helps you feel less stressed, anxious, or lonely in the moment, the part's work is done.

Although the strategy of these firefighting parts can be terrible (they are also the parts that get people addicted to opioids, use pornography, gamble, and do all kinds of risky, self-destructive behaviour), they mean well. This cycle—a hurt, young part getting triggered and a protector urgently getting rid of the pain—is called an "addictive process" in IFS. And the same basic process applies, whether you are using substances or activities to numb, avoid, or distract yourself from painful feelings.

This can be hard to understand, so let's use Grace* as an example. Grace was a middle-aged white woman who came to see me for help with her drinking. She was a successful marketing executive with a young family, so she could ill afford the regular hangovers that blighted her life. "Every Monday morning I wake up with a pounding headache and a cold sweat," she told me in our first session. "I always overdo it on Sunday nights, because I'm so stressed out about going back to work. Then it's a bottle or more of wine, which helps me de-stress but of course makes the next day a nightmare."

One of our early tasks was to translate Grace's suffering into parts language. I explained that she had a young part, Little Grace, who found her high-pressure job extremely stressful. We later learned that it also triggered memories of being under intense pressure from her high-flying, academic parents, making school and exams hellish for her. When this stressed little girl got triggered by the mammoth to-do list waiting for her on Monday morning, a firefighter stepped in to wash away all that stress with way too much Chardonnay.

One of the many ways in which IFS requires a paradigm shift from other therapies is that, in order to help Grace drink in moderation, we had to work with the wine-drinking firefighter, not try to get rid of it (the well-meaning approach of 12-step programmes). When I spoke to this part, I learned that it had developed when Grace was a child, getting her to eat sweets and zone out in front of the TV after a day of grinding through her studies, while Grace's parents criticised her harshly for any mistakes. This showed us that, like all protective parts, this one meant well, even if it was causing chaos in her life.

We got permission from the firefighter to help Little Grace, which we did using IFS's "healing steps"—a roadmap for connecting with, comforting, and ultimately healing hurt young parts like this. We transported her from the past to live with adult Grace in the present, joining her loving, rambunctious family, which made her very happy. Only then could we work with the firefighter on changing their approach, which they gladly did. After much debate about becoming entirely sober or cutting down, Grace chose the latter, so we came up with a plan to only drink on Friday and Saturday with dinner, and nothing on Sunday or during the week.

Because all her parts had bought into this strategy, Grace could stick to it with relative ease, unlike the get sober/relapse/get sober again cycle common to many models for treating addiction. She ended therapy feeling optimistic about her future and with all the skills she needed to keep checking in on both Little Grace and the drinking part, to make sure they were OK, especially when she had a wobble and felt like slipping back into her old patterns.

I hope that's helpful for you. If you are struggling with your drinking, or any other substance/activity that feels compulsive for you, please do seek help. It's always possible to heal early wounds and change these painkilling habits, so don't suffer in silence—life is too short to waste feeling bad about yourself and your choices.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

*All case studies in these posts are composites. I never tell the stories of real clients, as confidentiality is very important to me.
